questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 2 day history of a painful, swollen left breast with a burning sensation when her 10 day old daughter feeds. She has aches and feels feverish. There is a tender, warm, wedge-shaped area of erythema in the upper outer quadrant. No mass is palpable. Her temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 96 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A red, tender, warm wedge of breast with fever and flu-like aches in a breastfeeding mother, with no mass, is lactational mastitis. A fluctuant mass would point to abscess instead.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Breastfeeding, a red tender wedge, burning, fever and aches: inflammation of breast tissue. **No mass** rules out a collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Breastfeeding + red tender breast + fever, no lump = **lactational mastitis**.

elim: No palpable or fluctuant mass, so pus has not collected.
A condition of perimenopausal women with nipple discharge and retraction, not acute lactational redness and fever.
A painless, mobile lump without erythema or fever.
Rare, non-lactating, painless peau d'orange without fever; a 10 day postpartum woman with fever is mastitis.

steps.x: **E. Lactational mastitis.** Red, hot, tender breast while breastfeeding and no fluctuant lump = mastitis.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman, 5 weeks postpartum, has had a red, painful right breast for 8 days. Her GP advised continued feeding but she stopped feeding from that side because of pain. She now has a 4 cm exquisitely tender lump at 10 o'clock with overlying erythema, which is fluctuant on palpation. Her temperature is 38.6°C and pulse rate 104 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A fluctuant, tender, erythematous mass with fever after poorly managed mastitis is a breast abscess. Simple mastitis has no fluctuant mass.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Mastitis that was not managed well (feeding stopped, so milk stasis), now a **fluctuant** tender lump with fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluctuant red tender mass after untreated mastitis = **breast abscess**.

elim: Follows trauma, is firm and painless, and is not fluctuant or febrile.
A milk-filled cyst that is painless and not red, hot or febrile.
Painless diffuse peau d'orange without fever or a fluctuant lump.
Mastitis has no fluctuant mass; fluctuance means pus has collected.

steps.x: **A. Breast abscess.** Fluctuance is the key differentiator: abscess, not simple mastitis.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is breastfeeding has a breast abscess drained under ultrasound guidance. Gram stain of the aspirated pus shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Culture grows a coagulase-positive organism. Her temperature is 38.2°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Gram-positive cocci in clusters that are coagulase-positive are Staphylococcus aureus, the most common cause of both mastitis and breast abscess.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Clusters = staphylococci; coagulase-positive = **aureus**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The commonest organism for mastitis and abscess anyway: **S. aureus**.

elim: A yeast causing nipple thrush, not Gram-positive cocci or abscesses.
A Gram-negative rod; not a typical cause of lactational breast infection.
Coagulase-negative skin commensal, usually a contaminant.
Gram-positive cocci in chains and coagulase-negative.

steps.x: **C. Staphylococcus aureus.** Mastitis and breast abscess: think S. aureus first (which is why flucloxacillin is used).

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman attends her 6 week postnatal check. She is breastfeeding and asks what puts her at risk of the breast infection her sister had. She smokes 15 cigarettes a day, took folic acid in pregnancy, has never had breast problems and takes no medication. Her BMI is 24 kg/m². Her temperature is 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which feature of her history most increases her risk of mastitis?
questions.e: Smoking is a recognised risk factor for mastitis and breast abscess, alongside breastfeeding, cracked nipples and milk stasis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
She is breastfeeding (already at risk) and **smokes**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The only listed modifiable risk factor is **smoking**.

elim: A normal BMI; not a risk factor.
Absence of breast disease does not raise risk.
Not a risk factor for breast infection.
Not a risk factor.

steps.x: **C. Smoking.** Risk factors: childbearing age, breastfeeding, cracked nipples, milk stasis and smoking.

questions.stem: A 22 year old woman has had pain in her left breast for 1 day. She is breastfeeding her 3 week old son and has a cracked, sore left nipple. The left breast is swollen, with a red, tender segment and no lump. The right breast is normal. Her temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 100 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Unilateral, red, tender breast with fever in a breastfeeding woman with a cracked nipple is lactational mastitis. Engorgement is bilateral and afebrile.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: red, tender segment and no lump
steps.x: One breast, red tender segment, fever, a cracked nipple (portal of entry), no lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unilateral red breast + fever, no lump = **lactational mastitis**.

elim: No lump and only 1 day of symptoms; no collection.
Bilateral, diffuse fullness without fever or a red segment; this is one breast with fever.
A painless milk cyst, not a red, febrile breast.
Burning nipple pain without breast erythema or fever.

steps.x: **D. Lactational mastitis.** Engorgement is bilateral without fever; mastitis is one red, hot, tender area with fever.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman, 4 weeks postpartum, phones her GP with shivers, muscle aches and headache for 2 days. She thought she had flu. On further questioning she is breastfeeding and her right breast has become swollen and tender, with a burning pain during feeds and a little nipple discharge. She has no urinary symptoms and no abnormal vaginal loss. Her temperature is 38.3°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Flu-like symptoms with a swollen, tender breast, burning on feeding and nipple discharge in a breastfeeding mother are classic mastitis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: swollen and tender, with a burning pain during feeds
steps.x: Flu-like illness plus a **swollen, tender breast** with burning and discharge in a breastfeeding mother.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The breast is the source: **lactational mastitis**.

elim: Bilateral and without fever or flu-like illness.
Explains the aches but not a swollen, tender, burning breast.
Gives pelvic pain and offensive lochia; she has no abnormal vaginal loss.
No urinary symptoms; the breast signs are the source.

steps.x: **C. Lactational mastitis.** Always examine the breasts of a feverish breastfeeding mother with flu-like symptoms.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 4 month old daughter has a 6 day history of pain in her left breast. She smokes 20 cigarettes a day. There is a 3 cm red, hot, very tender periareolar swelling that is soft and fluctuant in the centre. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A fluctuant, red, very tender swelling with fever in a breastfeeding smoker is a breast abscess; fluctuance separates it from mastitis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: soft and fluctuant in the centre
steps.x: Breastfeeding and smoking are risk factors; a **fluctuant** tender red swelling with fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Fluctuant hot lump + fever = **breast abscess**.

elim: Painless diffuse peau d'orange without a fluctuant centre or fever.
Causes bloody nipple discharge, not a hot fluctuant swelling.
Mastitis has no fluctuant mass.
Superficial thrombophlebitis: a tender cord, not a fluctuant lump.

steps.x: **A. Breast abscess.** Fluctuant swelling = pus = abscess.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman who is breastfeeding has had a red, painful right breast for 4 days and has not sought help. Today she is shaking and drowsy. The redness spreads beyond the breast. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 86/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
questions.q: Which finding most indicates that she needs emergency treatment?
questions.e: Hypotension with tachycardia, high fever and drowsiness means sepsis from spreading breast infection: an emergency needing the sepsis bundle.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Systemically unwell, spreading infection, drowsy, tachycardic and **hypotensive**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: This is **sepsis**; the hypotension is the red flag that makes it an emergency.

elim: Long duration alone does not define an emergency.
Breastfeeding should continue; it is not a danger sign.
Acceptable saturation; not the key danger sign.
Pain is expected in mastitis and does not mark severity.

steps.x: **A. BP 86/50 mmHg.** Systemic illness or spreading infection in mastitis = think sepsis, an emergency.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman, 7 weeks postpartum, presents with a painful lump in her right breast. Two weeks ago she had a red, tender breast with fever but did not see a doctor and stopped feeding from that side. The lump is 3 cm, tender, red and fluctuant. Her temperature is 38.1°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of the lump?
o: Blocked duct from a tight bra
questions.e: A breast abscess is typically a complication of untreated or inadequately treated puerperal mastitis, as here.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.

clues: did not see a doctor and stopped feeding from that side
steps.x: Previous untreated mastitis, milk stasis, then a **fluctuant** tender lump.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: This is an abscess, and its cause is **untreated mastitis**.

elim: A blocked duct gives a tender lump without a fluctuant collection or fever.
A painless, hard, irregular lump, not hot, fluctuant and febrile.
No trauma, and fat necrosis is firm, not fluctuant.
Affects perimenopausal women with discharge and retraction.

steps.x: **E. Untreated lactational mastitis.** Breast abscess is the complication of untreated or inadequately treated puerperal mastitis.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 2 week old son has a 2 day history of a red, sore left breast with flu-like symptoms. Her midwife worries about a collection. On examination there is diffuse redness and tenderness of the lower outer quadrant. The breast is firm but there is no discrete or fluctuant mass. Her temperature is 37.9°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diffuse redness and tenderness without a fluctuant mass in a breastfeeding mother is mastitis; fluctuance would be needed to call it an abscess.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name what this patient has or shows before reading the options.
Red, tender breast with flu-like illness while breastfeeding, but **no fluctuant mass**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Without fluctuance this is **mastitis**, not abscess.

elim: Needs a fluctuant mass; none is present.
A smooth, painless, discrete lump without redness or fever.
A painless, mobile discrete lump.
An eczematous nipple change, not a red tender quadrant with fever.

steps.x: **D. Lactational mastitis.** No fluctuant mass = mastitis; fluctuant mass = abscess.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 8 week old son has been taking oral flucloxacillin for 6 days for mastitis. Her right breast remains painful and her fever has returned. There is a tender, red area in the upper outer quadrant with a possible deep fluctuant area. Her temperature is 38.4°C and pulse rate 100 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: Suspected breast abscess (fever and a possible fluctuant area despite antibiotics) is confirmed with breast ultrasound, the gold standard, which can also guide aspiration.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
Mastitis not settling on antibiotics with a **possible fluctuant** area: suspect abscess.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Confirm a suspected abscess with **breast ultrasound**.

elim: Useful if septic but cannot show a collection.
For suspected tumours, not an infected collection.
Painful and less useful in the dense lactating breast; ultrasound shows fluid.
Not first choice; ultrasound is quick, cheap and the gold standard here.

steps.x: **B. Breast ultrasound.** Mastitis is clinical; suspected abscess = breast ultrasound (gold standard).

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 3 week old daughter has a 1 day history of a tender, red right breast. She feels achy. There is a warm, tender red patch and no lump. Her nipples are intact. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg. A junior doctor wants to request tests to confirm mastitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: Uncomplicated mastitis is a clinical diagnosis; tests are reserved for suspected abscess (ultrasound) or systemic illness.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
Early, mild mastitis: no lump, intact nipples, well.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: No test is needed: **clinical diagnosis**.

elim: She is not septic; cultures add nothing.
Only if an abscess is suspected (a fluctuant mass).
Not used to diagnose mastitis in a lactating breast.
Does not change management; mastitis is a clinical diagnosis.

steps.x: **D. No investigation; diagnose clinically.** Mastitis is diagnosed clinically; scan only if you suspect an abscess.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman who is breastfeeding has mastitis that has not improved after 48 hours of oral flucloxacillin. This is her third episode in 4 months. She is well apart from breast pain. There is a tender red area but no fluctuant lump. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Recurrent mastitis or failure to respond to antibiotics warrants breast milk culture to identify the organism and its sensitivities (for example MRSA), guiding antibiotics.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: not improved after 48 hours of oral flucloxacillin
steps.x: Recurrent and not responding to flucloxacillin, no lump (so no abscess to scan for).

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Find the organism and its sensitivities: **milk culture**.

elim: No role in recurrent mastitis without a mass.
Used for suspicious solid lumps, not infection.
Irrelevant to breast infection.
Not helpful in the lactating breast without a mass.

steps.x: **A. Breast milk culture and sensitivity.** Mastitis is clinical, but recurrent or non-responding infection needs milk culture.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman with a BMI of 38 kg/m² is breastfeeding her 6 week old son. She has a 5 day history of a painful, red left breast and fever despite flucloxacillin. The breast is large and tender, so it is impossible to tell clinically whether there is a fluctuant collection. Her temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to guide management?
questions.e: When abscess is suspected but cannot be confirmed by examination, breast ultrasound is the gold standard and guides aspiration or drainage.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).

clues: impossible to tell clinically whether there is a fluctuant collection
steps.x: Mastitis failing antibiotics, abscess possible, examination unhelpful.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Image to find pus: **breast ultrasound**, which can then guide aspiration.

elim: Identifies organisms but cannot show whether there is pus to drain.
A blind aspirate may miss the collection; image it first.
Less useful in the dense lactating breast and does not guide aspiration.
Does not show a collection.

steps.x: **B. Breast ultrasound.** Suspected abscess = ultrasound; it also guides aspiration.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is breastfeeding presents with 3 days of a red, painful left breast. She is now confused. Her temperature is 39.3°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 88/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 96% breathing air. There is spreading erythema over the left chest wall.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: She has sepsis from spreading breast infection. Blood cultures (with lactate) are taken immediately, before IV antibiotics, as part of the sepsis bundle.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide which test answers the exact question asked (initial or diagnostic).
Confused, hypotensive, tachycardic with spreading infection: **sepsis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sepsis bundle starts with **blood cultures** before antibiotics.

elim: May be needed later, but sepsis comes first: cultures then immediate antibiotics.
No role in acute infection.
Not the first test in sepsis from a breast source.
No role in acute sepsis.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Systemically unwell mastitis = sepsis pathway: cultures, lactate, IV antibiotics, fluids.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 1 day history of a painful, red area on her right breast. She is breastfeeding her 5 week old son. She asks whether she should stop feeding from the right breast to protect her baby. There is no lump and her nipples are intact. Her temperature is 37.7°C and pulse rate 88 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Express and discard milk from the right breast
Stop feeding from the right breast for 1 week
Stop feeding until antibiotics are finished
questions.e: Breastfeeding should continue from both breasts: emptying the breast clears the infected duct, and the milk is not harmful to the baby.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: stop feeding from the right breast
steps.x: Early mastitis, no lump. She wants to stop feeding from the affected side.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: First-line is to **continue breastfeeding** with milk expression.

elim: Unnecessary: the milk is not harmful to the infant.
Stopping causes milk stasis and makes mastitis and abscess more likely.
Milk stasis worsens the infection.
Antibiotics are not yet needed and stopping feeds worsens stasis.

steps.x: **A. Continue feeding from both breasts.** Mastitis: keep feeding (or expressing) from the affected breast.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman has mastitis in her left breast. She is breastfeeding her 2 week old daughter and continues to feed regularly. She asks for something for the pain and fever. She has no allergies and no history of asthma or peptic ulcer. Her temperature is 38.0°C and pulse rate 92 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate analgesia?
questions.e: Supportive care in mastitis uses simple analgesia: paracetamol or ibuprofen, both safe in breastfeeding.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: no history of asthma or peptic ulcer
steps.x: Breastfeeding mother needing analgesia and an antipyretic, no NSAID contraindications.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Simple analgesia: paracetamol or **ibuprofen**.

elim: Avoided while breastfeeding (Reye's syndrome risk in the infant).
Avoided in breastfeeding: risk of opioid toxicity in the infant.
Excessive for mastitis and passes into milk.
An opioid; not needed and best avoided in breastfeeding.

steps.x: **C. Ibuprofen.** Mastitis supportive care: paracetamol or ibuprofen, continue feeding.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who is breastfeeding has a tender, red right breast. Over the last 24 hours she has fed and expressed effectively from both sides, but the pain and redness are unchanged. There is no lump. She has no drug allergies. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: No improvement after 12 to 24 hours of effective milk expression is the trigger for antibiotics: flucloxacillin for 10 days, covering S. aureus.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: Over the last 24 hours she has fed and expressed effectively
steps.x: Effective expression for 24 hours and **no improvement**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Step up to antibiotics: **flucloxacillin 10 days**.

elim: For MRSA or severe illness; she is systemically well.
Not reliable against beta-lactamase producing S. aureus, and too short.
Too short; the course is 10 days.
A urinary antiseptic with no role in breast infection.

steps.x: **C. Oral flucloxacillin for 10 days.** No better after 12 to 24 hours of expression = flucloxacillin for 10 days.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman who is breastfeeding her 10 day old son has a painful left breast that started this morning. Her left nipple has a deep fissure with yellow crusting and surrounding redness. The left breast has a red, tender segment and no lump. She has no allergies. Her temperature is 37.9°C and pulse rate 90 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Continue feeding and review in 48 hours
Continue feeding and start oral flucloxacillin
Stop feeding from the left breast
questions.e: An infected nipple fissure is an indication for antibiotics without waiting 12 to 24 hours: flucloxacillin for 10 days, while continuing to feed.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Early mastitis but with an **infected nipple fissure**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: That skips the wait: **start flucloxacillin** and keep feeding.

elim: An infected nipple fissure is an indication for antibiotics now.
Causes milk stasis and makes things worse.
Treats candida; this is a bacterial (crusting) fissure.
There is no abscess (no lump).

steps.x: **B. Continue feeding and start oral flucloxacillin.** Antibiotic triggers: no better after 12 to 24 hours, infected nipple fissure, systemically unwell, or positive cultures.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman who is breastfeeding has a 2.5 cm breast abscess confirmed on ultrasound. She had anaphylaxis to penicillin as a child. Her temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. The breast surgeons have seen her.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Stop breastfeeding and give oral clarithromycin
questions.e: Definitive treatment of a breast abscess is drainage (ultrasound-guided aspiration or incision and drainage) with continued antibiotics; clarithromycin replaces flucloxacillin in penicillin allergy.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.

clues: 2.5 cm breast abscess confirmed on ultrasound
steps.x: Confirmed abscess, so it needs **drainage**; penicillin anaphylaxis rules out flucloxacillin.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Drain it and cover with **clarithromycin**.

elim: A walled-off abscess does not resolve with antibiotics alone; it needs draining.
Contains a penicillin (anaphylaxis) and does not drain the pus.
Stopping feeding is unnecessary and worsens stasis; no drainage.
Flucloxacillin is a penicillin; she had anaphylaxis.

steps.x: **D. Ultrasound-guided aspiration and oral clarithromycin.** Abscess = drain (aspiration or I&D) + continue antibiotics; clarithromycin if penicillin allergic.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman who is breastfeeding sees her GP with a 5 day history of right breast pain despite flucloxacillin. There is a 4 cm red, tender, fluctuant mass at 2 o'clock. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. She feels unwell but is alert.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Stop breastfeeding from the right breast
Urgent referral to the general surgeons
questions.e: A significant breast abscess (fluctuant mass with fever despite antibiotics) needs urgent referral to the general surgeons for drainage.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
A significant abscess failing antibiotics in primary care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Pus needs draining: **urgent surgical referral**.

elim: A significant abscess will not settle with antibiotics alone.
Too slow; a significant abscess needs urgent drainage.
Unhelpful; stasis worsens infection.
Changing antibiotic does not drain pus.

steps.x: **E. Urgent referral to the general surgeons.** Significant abscess = urgent referral to general surgeons for drainage.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman who is breastfeeding is brought to the Emergency Department with a 4 day history of a red, painful left breast. She is drowsy. Her temperature is 39.5°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 84/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 25 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 94% breathing air. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation
Referral to the breast clinic in 2 weeks
questions.e: Spreading breast infection with hypotension and raised lactate is sepsis, an emergency: cultures, IV antibiotics and IV fluids within the hour.

steps.x: A management question: work out where the patient is on the treatment ladder, then pick the next step.
Hypotensive, tachycardic, drowsy, lactate above 4: **septic shock**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Sepsis bundle: **IV antibiotics and fluids** now.

elim: Oral treatment is inadequate in septic shock.
Supportive care alone is inadequate in sepsis.
Sepsis is an emergency.
No abscess is described, and sepsis needs antibiotics within the hour.

steps.x: **A. IV antibiotics and IV fluid resuscitation.** Systemically unwell mastitis = sepsis emergency: IV antibiotics and fluids.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman develops a red, tender left breast. Her 4 week old son has been sleepy and she has been feeding him only every 6 to 7 hours, mostly from the right side. The left breast feels engorged. Her temperature is 38.0°C.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism leading to her mastitis?
o: Haematogenous spread of bacteria from the uterus
Hormonal hyperplasia of a breast lobule
Squamous metaplasia of the lactiferous duct
Stagnant milk acting as a nidus for bacterial growth
questions.e: Infrequent or ineffective feeding causes engorgement and milk stasis, which gives bacteria a nidus to colonise and drives inflammation.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
Infrequent feeds from the left side: **milk stasis** and engorgement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Stagnant milk is a **nidus** for bacteria.

elim: Not the mechanism of lactational mastitis.
Mastitis is local, not blood-borne.
That describes fibroadenoma.
Linked to periductal mastitis in smokers, not stasis.

steps.x: **E. Stagnant milk acting as a nidus for bacterial growth.** Milk stasis is a nidus for bacterial colonisation and inflammation.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman, 2 weeks postpartum, has painful cracked nipples because her son has a poor latch. She develops a hot, red, tender right breast with fever. Culture of expressed milk grows Staphylococcus aureus.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for how the organism entered the breast?
o: Ascending from the axillary lymph nodes
Blood-borne spread from a urinary infection
Contamination from the gut via the portal vein
Spread from the uterus after delivery
Through the nipple fissures from the infant's mouth
questions.e: Cracked nipples give S. aureus from the infant's oral flora (and skin) a portal of entry into breast tissue.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.
Cracked nipples from a poor latch, then S. aureus mastitis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The cracks are the **portal of entry** for organisms from the baby's mouth.

elim: Lymph drains away from the breast, not into it.
Mastitis is not usually haematogenous.
No route to the breast.
Endometritis does not seed the breast.

steps.x: **E. Through the nipple fissures from the infant's mouth.** Cracked nipples = portal of entry for S. aureus from the infant's mouth.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman had mastitis 10 days ago and stopped feeding from the affected breast. She took only 2 days of her flucloxacillin. She now has a 3 cm fluctuant, tender lump. Ultrasound shows a walled-off fluid collection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the change in her condition?
o: Malignant change in an inflamed duct
Resistance of the organism to all antibiotics
Thrombosis of a superficial breast vein
Unresolved inflammation forming a localised pus collection
questions.e: Inadequately treated mastitis lets inflammation persist and coalesce into a walled-off pus collection (abscess), which will not resolve with antibiotics alone.

steps.x: A science question: explain the mechanism behind the finding in the stem.

clues: stopped feeding from the affected breast
took only 2 days of her flucloxacillin
steps.x: Inadequate treatment and milk stasis, then a **walled-off** collection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Unresolved inflammation has **coalesced into an abscess**.

elim: Mastitis does not turn into cancer.
A galactocele is a painless milk cyst, not a tender infected collection.
The problem is that she stopped treatment early, not pan-resistance.
That is Mondor disease.

steps.x: **E. Unresolved inflammation forming a localised pus collection.** Unresolved mastitis coalesces into a walled-off abscess that needs drainage.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman with mastitis is advised to keep breastfeeding from the affected breast. Her partner is worried that the milk is infected and will harm their 3 week old daughter. Her temperature is 37.8°C.
questions.q: Which is the best explanation for continuing breastfeeding?
o: Breastfeeding raises maternal oestrogen to fight infection
Emptying the breast clears the infected duct and the milk is safe
It is only advised once antibiotics have sterilised the milk
Milk contains antibiotics produced by the breast
questions.e: Continuing to feed empties the breast, clearing the infected duct and relieving stasis, and the milk is not harmful to the infant.
